claims.claim: Existence of a 2-factor, and an explicit 2-factor when one exists, can be determined in polynomial time.
claims.evidence: If some vertex has degree below two, no 2-factor is possible. Otherwise, every perfect matching in the stated gadget must match all d(v)−2 private dummies at v to distinct incidence vertices, leaving exactly two incidences at v to be matched through original-edge links. Those links therefore form a spanning 2-regular subgraph. Conversely, a 2-factor matches its selected incidences through edge links and leaves exactly d(v)−2 incidences at each vertex, which can be bijectively matched to the private dummies. The gadget has O(n^2) vertices and O(n^3) edges, so general-graph perfect matching gives a polynomial algorithm and an explicit factor. The checker independently confirmed the equivalence for every simple graph through five vertices.
claims.search_method: Bidirectional gadget proof plus exhaustive exact enumeration of the gadget characterization.

claims.claim: If the 2-factor routine reports that none exists, returning (G,nil) is correct.
claims.evidence: A Hamiltonian cycle is itself a spanning 2-regular subgraph. Thus a graph without a 2-factor cannot be Hamiltonian, making nil correct without any edit. The checker exhaustively confirmed this implication through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Direct contrapositive of the definition, supplemented by exhaustive exact graph enumeration.

claims.claim: If G has a 2-factor with q cycle components, one can add at most q edges and explicitly obtain a Hamiltonian cycle; if G is connected, at most q−1 additions suffice.
claims.evidence: For the general bound, omit one witness edge from each factor cycle, producing q disjoint spanning paths, and cyclically join their endpoints. At most q absent connectors must be added; for q=1 the original cycle already works. If G is connected, start with one factor cycle D. Until all vertices are included, connectivity supplies an original edge xy from D to another factor cycle C. Omitting witness edges xx′ and yy′ and using xy together with x′y′ merges the two cycles; only x′y′ can require an addition. Repeating performs q−1 merges. The omitted edges remain in the graph and are merely unused by the witness. Exhaustive checks through six vertices confirmed both addition bounds for every graph and every contained 2-factor.
claims.search_method: Explicit endpoint-splicing proof, cut analysis for connected graphs, and exact exhaustive enumeration.

claims.claim: For every fixed real 0<c≤3, Sidestep(Hamiltonian Cycle,dist_e,n/c) is in FP.
claims.evidence: Disconnected graphs and graphs without a 2-factor are correctly returned unchanged with nil. Otherwise G is connected and has a 2-factor whose q components each contain at least three vertices, so q≤floor(n/3). The connected splice adds at most q−1≤n/3≤n/c edges and supplies an explicit Hamiltonian cycle. Small n can be decided directly. Every operation is polynomial and keeps the labeled vertex set fixed. Exact enumeration through six vertices checked the nil branches, component bound, and endpoint c=3 inequality.
claims.search_method: Complete branch-by-branch algorithm audit and exact boundary enumeration at the strongest endpoint c=3.

claims.claim: For arbitrary fixed c>0, the target is polynomially solvable on graphs whose girth is at least c.
claims.evidence: The disconnected and no-2-factor nil branches remain sound. If a 2-factor exists in a graph of finite girth g≥c, every factor cycle has length at least g, hence qg≤n and q≤n/c. On a connected input, the splice needs at most q−1≤q additions. Acyclic graphs necessarily take the no-factor branch. Thus the promised class is handled in polynomial time. The checker exhaustively verified the girth/component inequality through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Promise-class proof using minimum cycle length, with exact exhaustive girth checks.

claims.claim: A general cheap non-Hamiltonicity edit is obtained from a component-count obstruction.
claims.evidence: After deleting all edges between the stated parts, H−S has at least p components. If S is nonempty and H had a Hamiltonian cycle, removing S from that cycle would leave at most |S| path components; adding other H-edges cannot increase this count. If S is empty, a Hamiltonian graph must be connected. Since p>max{1,|S|}, both cases contradict Hamiltonicity. The number of edits is exactly the number of deleted cross-part edges, assumed at most n/c. The checker exhaustively verified the underlying separator condition for every Hamiltonian graph through six vertices.
claims.search_method: Direct separator/component proof plus exhaustive exact testing of the Hamiltonian necessary condition.

claims.claim: For every c, any graph with a vertex of degree at most n/c admits a polynomial-time valid nil output within radius n/c.
claims.evidence: Deleting every edge incident with v makes exactly deg(v) edits, which is at most n/c by hypothesis. The resulting graph has an isolated vertex and is non-Hamiltonian; exceptional tiny orders can be decided directly. Finding v and deleting its incident edges are polynomial-time operations. The checker verified exact edit counts and non-Hamiltonicity for every graph through six vertices across an exact rational grid of c values.
claims.search_method: Explicit isolation construction and exact exhaustive edit-count checks.

claims.claim: A sublinear-component 2-factor routine would settle the full target for every fixed c.
claims.evidence: Let the routine's factor have at most b(n)=o(n) components on Hamiltonian inputs. For fixed c choose N with b(n)−1≤n/c for n≥N; orders below N are decidable by constant-size exhaustive search. For larger inputs, first return nil on disconnected graphs or graphs without a factor. On a connected graph with returned factor size q, splice when q−1≤n/c. If q−1>n/c, Hamiltonicity would imply q≤b(n), hence q−1≤b(n)−1≤n/c, a contradiction, so returning (G,nil) is sound. This gives a polynomial algorithm for each fixed c. The checker verified the exact threshold implication over an integer/rational grid.
claims.search_method: Quantifier and contrapositive audit of the conditional reduction, supplemented by exact threshold checks.

claims.claim: For every c>3, high minimum degree alone cannot guarantee a Hamiltonian graph within n/c edits.
claims.evidence: For c>3 the interval (1/c,(1−1/c)/2) is nonempty; choose rational α there and take infinitely many n with a=αn integral, b=n−a, and G=K_{a,b}. Then δ(G)=a>n/c. In any cyclic ordering, if x and z count B-B and A-A consecutive pairs, incidence counting gives x−z=b−a, so at least b−a absent same-part edges must be added to support a Hamiltonian cycle. Conversely, arranging the B vertices into a nonempty blocks separated by the a A vertices uses exactly b−a B-B edges, proving the edit distance is b−a=(1−2α)n>n/c. The checker verified exact rational witness inequalities and exhaustively confirmed the cyclic-word identity and minimum through length twelve.
claims.search_method: Exact extremal construction, cyclic incidence counting, matching upper construction, and integer-only finite checks.

claims.claim: The n/3 component bound for an arbitrary 2-factor remains tight even under the promise that the graph is Hamiltonian.
claims.evidence: For every q≥2, partition 3q vertices into q triples, include each triple's triangle, and add a cyclic ordering that interleaves the triples so adjacent vertices always come from different triples. The added ordering is an explicit Hamiltonian cycle, while the q disjoint triangles remain a 2-factor with q=n/3 components. Thus a Hamiltonian graph can contain a 2-factor attaining the general upper bound. The checker constructed and verified these graphs exactly for q=2 through q=12.
claims.search_method: Explicit infinite construction with exact verification of both witnesses.

target_evidence: The exact target requires a proof or disproof for every fixed c>0 on every labeled graph. The draft gives a complete algorithm only for 0<c≤3, plus correct algorithms or certificates for restricted classes and a conditional sufficient reduction. Its complete-bipartite family is explicitly only a barrier to the high-minimum-degree proof method: those graphs themselves have an immediate correct nil certificate, so the family does not disprove the target. No argument resolves the unrestricted c>3 cases. The progress is nevertheless material and correct, so target coverage is VALID_PARTIAL_PROGRESS. The final writeup expressly says the universal statement remains unresolved for c>3 and labels the resolution PARTIAL; therefore claimed_resolution is ACCURATE, neither overstated nor understated.
